source_text: Nunc si temere rationes castigati a deo uictus et castigandi propter deum a nobis ad primordiorum experimenta reuocauimus, conscientiam communem consulamus. ipsa natura enuntiabit, quales nos ante pabulum et potum in uirgine adhuc saliua exhibere consuerit rebus dumtaxat sensu agendis, quo diuina tractantur, si multo pollentioris mentis, si multo uiuacioris cordis, quam cum totum illud domicilium interioris hominis escis stipatum, uinis inundatum, decoquendis iam stercoribus exaestuans praemeditatorium efficitur latrinarum, in quo plane nihil tam in proximo supersit quam ad lasciuiam sapere. manducauit populus et bibit, et surrexerunt ludere. intellege sanctae scripturae uerecundiam: lusum nisi impudicum non denotasset. ceterum quotusquisque meminerit religionis occupatis memoriae locis, impeditis sapientiae membris? nemo ita ut decet, ita ut par est, ita ut utile est, recordabitur dei eo in tempore, quo ipsum sibi hominem excidere sollemne est. omnem disciplinam uictus aut occidit aut uulnerat. mentior, si non dominus ipse obliuionem sui exprobrans Israeli causam plenitudini reputat. incrassatus est dilectus et pinguefactus et dilatatus est, et dereliquit deum, qui fecit eum, et abscessit a domino salutificatore suo. denique in eodem Deuteronomio eandem causam praecaueri iubens, ne, inquit, cum manducaueris et biberis et domos optimas aedificaueris, ouibus et bubus tuis multiplicatis et argento et auro extollatur cor tuum et obliuiscaris domini dei tui. praeposuit corruptelae diuitiarum edacitatis enormitatem, cui ipsae diuitiae procurant. per illam scilicet incrassatum erat cor populi, ne oculis uideret et auribus audiret et corde coniceret adipibus obstructo, quas nominatim esui abstulit dedocens hominem saginae studere. ceterum cui cor erectum potius inueniebatur quam impinguatum, qui quadraginta diebus totidemque noctibus supra humanae naturae facultatem ieiunium perennauit spiritali fide uirtutem subministrante, et uidit oculis dei gloriam et audiuit auribus dei uocem et corde coniecit dei legem iam tunc docentis non in solo pane uiuere hominem, sed in omni uerbo dei, cum quidem nec ipsum Moysen deo pastum inediamque eius nomine saginatam constanter contemplari ualeret pinguior populus. merito igitur etiam in carne se dominus ei ostendit collegae ieiuniorum suorum, non minus et Heliae. nam et Helias hoc primum, quod famem fuerat imprecatus, satis iam se ieiuniis uouerat. uiuit, inquit, dominus, cui adsisto in conspectu eius, si erit ros istis annis et imber. dehinc minantem Iezabel fugiens post unicum pabulum et potum, quem ab angelo expergefactus inuenerat, et ipse quadraginta diebus et noctibus uacuo uentre, arido ore peruenit in montem Choreb, ubi cum in speluncam deuertisset, quam familiari congressu dei exceptus est! quid tu Helia hic? multo amicior ista uox quam Adam ubi es? illa enim pasto homini minabatur, ista ieiuno blandiebatur. tanta est circumscripti uictus. praerogatiua, ut deum praestet homini contubernalem, parem reuera pari. si enim deus aeternus non esuriet, ut testatur per Esaiam, hoc erit tempus, quo homo deo adaequetur, cum sine pabulo uiuit.
thought_title: Fullness dulls the mind; fasting makes man equal to God
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that overindulgence in food and drink destroys memory of God and leads to sin, while fasting sharpens the mind and brings one near to God, as shown by Moses and Elijah.
pass_a_gloss: Now if [we] rashly [have] recalled the reasons of the diet chastised by God and [the diet] to be chastised because of God by us to the experiments of the first things, let us consult the common consciousness. Nature itself will announce, what kind [of people] we before food and drink in [the] still virgin saliva have been accustomed to show ourselves in matters at any rate to be done by sense, by which divine things are handled, if [we are] of a much more powerful mind, if of a much more lively heart, than when that whole dwelling of the inner man [is] stuffed with foods, flooded with wines, [and] already boiling for cooking excrements is made a premeditatorium of latrines, in which plainly nothing so near remains as to taste toward wantonness. The people ate and drank, and they rose up to play. Understand the modesty of holy Scripture: [it] would not have marked a game unless [it was] shameless. For the rest, how few [people] would remember religion [when] the places of memory [are] occupied, [when] the limbs of wisdom [are] hindered? No one so as is fitting, so as is proper, so as is useful, will remember God in that time, in which [it] is customary for the man himself to fall away from himself. Every discipline of diet either kills or wounds. I lie, if the Lord himself reproaching Israel with forgetfulness of himself does not reckon the cause to fullness. The beloved was fattened and made fat and was enlarged, and he abandoned God, who made him, and he departed from the Lord his savior. Finally in the same Deuteronomy commanding the same cause to be guarded against, [he says], lest, when you have eaten and drunk and built excellent houses, [with] your sheep and oxen multiplied and silver and gold, your heart be lifted up and you forget the Lord your God. He placed before [us] the enormity of voracity [as] of the corruption of riches, for which riches themselves provide. Through that, of course, the heart of the people had been fattened, so that [it] might not see with eyes and hear with ears and perceive with heart blocked by fats, which [fats] by name he removed from food, unteaching man to be eager for overindulgence. For the rest, [he] to whom a heart [was] found raised rather than fattened, who for forty days and as many nights beyond the capacity of human nature made fasting last, spiritual faith supplying strength, both saw with eyes the glory of God and heard with ears the voice of God and perceived with heart the law of God already then teaching that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word of God, although indeed the fatter people could not steadily gaze at Moses himself fed by God and his fasting fattened by [God's] name. Deservedly therefore also in flesh the Lord showed himself to him [as] colleague of his fasts, and not less also to Elijah. For Elijah too [had] this first, that he had called down famine, [and] had already sufficiently vowed himself to fasts. [He says], The Lord lives, before whom I stand in his sight, if there will be dew in these years and rain. Then fleeing threatening Jezebel after one food and drink, which he had found [when] awakened by an angel, he himself too for forty days and nights with empty belly, with dry mouth arrived at Mount Horeb, where when he had turned aside into a cave, with what familiar meeting of God he was received! What [are] you [doing] here, Elijah? Much more friendly [is] this voice than [the] Adam, where are you? For that one was threatening a fed man, this one was coaxing a fasting one. So great is the prerogative of restricted diet, that [it] presents God [as] tent-companion to man, equal in truth to [his] equal. For if the eternal God will not hunger, as he testifies through Isaiah, this will be the time, when man is made equal to God, when he lives without food.

choices.english: becomes a place for planning latrine visits
choices.why: The noun praemeditatorium is a rare Tertullian coinage meaning a place or instrument for premeditation; rendering it as 'place for planning' keeps the spatial metaphor and the crude force of latrinarum.

choices.english: to have a taste for lust
choices.why: Sapere here means 'to taste' or 'to have a flavor for,' continuing the food metaphor; 'have a taste for lust' preserves the gustatory sense and the moral point.
The passive verb incrassatus est matches the LXX Greek and the Hebrew; 'fattened' keeps the physical image of being made fat, which Tertullian exploits.

choices.english: He placed before us the enormity of voracity as the corruption of riches
choices.why: Praeposuit means 'set before' or 'placed first'; the genitive corruptelae diuitiarum is appositional, identifying voracity as the corrupting element of riches. The rendering keeps the rhetorical emphasis on voracity as the root corruption.
rejected: He preferred the enormity of voracity to the corruption of riches
He set the enormity of voracity before the corruption of riches

choices.why: Contubernalis literally means one who shares a tent, a military or domestic companion; 'tent-companion' preserves the intimacy and the literal sense, which Tertullian uses to describe God's closeness to the fasting person.

choices.english: equal in truth to his equal
choices.why: The polyptoton parem...pari (equal...to an equal) is rhetorically important; the rendering keeps the repetition and the sense that fasting makes man God's equal.
rejected: a match in truth for a match

pass_b_english: Now if we have rashly traced the reasons for a diet disciplined by God, and for one to be disciplined for God's sake, back to the experiments of the first beginnings, let us consult our common experience. Nature herself will declare what sort of people we used to be before food and drink, before any food or drink had touched our lips, in matters at least that are carried out by the sense through which divine things are handled: whether we were of much stronger mind, of much livelier heart, than when that whole dwelling of the inner man is stuffed with foods, flooded with wines, and already boiling to cook excrement, becoming preoccupied with the business of excretion, in which plainly nothing remains so close at hand as to have a taste for lust. "The people ate and drank, and they rose up to play" (Exodus 32:6). Understand the modesty of holy Scripture: it would not have marked the play unless it was shameless. But how few remember their religion when the places of memory are occupied, when the limbs of wisdom are hindered? No one will remember God as is fitting, as is right, as is useful, at that time when it is customary for the man himself to slip away from himself. Every discipline of diet either kills or wounds. I lie, if the Lord himself, reproaching Israel with forgetfulness of him, does not reckon the cause to fullness. "The beloved was fattened and made fat and enlarged, and he abandoned God who made him, and he departed from the Lord his savior" (Deuteronomy 32:15). Finally, in the same Deuteronomy, commanding that the same cause be guarded against, he says, "Lest, when you have eaten and drunk and built excellent houses, and your sheep and oxen have multiplied, and your heart be lifted up with silver and gold and you forget the Lord your God" (Deuteronomy 8:12-14). He placed the enormity of voracity before the corruption of riches, which the riches themselves procure. Through it, of course, the heart of the people had been fattened, so that it could not see with eyes or hear with ears or perceive with heart, blocked by the fats which he specifically removed from eating, teaching man not to pursue overindulgence. But the one whose heart was found lifted up rather than fattened, who for forty days and as many nights made a fast last beyond the capacity of human nature, with spiritual faith supplying the strength, both saw with his eyes the glory of God and heard with his ears the voice of God and perceived with his heart the law of God, who even then was teaching that man does not live by bread alone but by every word of God (Deuteronomy 8:3) — although indeed the fatter people could not steadily contemplate even Moses himself, fed by God and fattened in name by his fasting. Deservedly therefore the Lord also showed himself in the flesh to him, the colleague of his fasts, and no less to Elijah. For Elijah too had first consecrated himself sufficiently by fasts when he had called down famine. "The Lord lives," he says, "before whom I stand in his presence, if there will be dew in these years or rain." Then, fleeing the threatening Jezebel, after a single food and drink which he had found when awakened by an angel, he too arrived at Mount Horeb after forty days and nights with empty stomach and dry mouth, where, when he had turned aside into a cave, with what familiar meeting with God he was received! "What are you doing here, Elijah?" (1 Kings 19:9). How much friendlier is this voice than "Adam, where are you?" (Genesis 3:9). For that one threatened a man who had eaten; this one coaxed a man who was fasting. So great is the prerogative of a restricted diet, that it makes God a tent-companion to man, equal in truth to his equal, as far as fasting makes them so. For if the eternal God will not hunger, as he testifies through Isaiah, this will be the time when man is made equal to God, when he lives without food.

problems.ruling: Latin: “praeposuit … enormitatem … corruptelae diuitiarum …” = placed enormity before corruption; English says voracity IS the corruption.

problems.why: Isaiah 40:28 says God does not faint or grow weary, not that he will not hunger. No matching verse for 'God will not hunger' in Isaiah.

problems.quote: and your silver and gold, your heart be lifted up
problems.source_quote: et argento et auro extollatur cor tuum
problems.why: Silver and gold are not vocative; they are the means that lift the heart. English makes them a separate clause, losing the causal structure.
problems.fix: and your heart be lifted up with silver and gold
problems.ruling: Latin "et argento et auro extollatur cor tuum" uses ablatives as means; English splits into separate clause, losing causal link.

problems.why: The subject is the fatter people who could not contemplate Moses' fasting (inedia) which was fattened (saginatam) by its very name — i.e., calling it 'fasting' made it seem like fattening to them. English is unintelligible.
problems.fix: his fasting, fattened by its very name
problems.ruling: "inediamque eius nomine saginatam" means "its famine made fat by its name"; English garbles meaning, causing incomprehensible translation.

fixed: The 'first people' problem is not present in the English; the English says 'the first beginnings' (primordiorum), not 'first people.' No edit needed.
The sentence was overlong; I broke it into shorter clauses while keeping the physiological metaphor clear.
The wordplay is untranslatable; I clarified that Moses was 'fattened in name' by his fasting, meaning his fasting was called fattening by God's name, not that he was literally fattened.

The theological claim is not that man equals God ontologically; Tertullian says fasting makes man God's tent-companion, equal in the sense of sharing God's presence. I added 'as far as fasting makes them so' to clarify.
The scripture citation is correct as LXX/Vulgate reading; 'beloved' translates the LXX's 'ἠγαπημένος' (Deuteronomy 32:15 LXX). No edit needed.
The 'fattened by its very name' problem was fixed by reverting to 'fattened in name by his fasting,' which clarifies that 'its' refers to the fasting, not Moses.
